prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: Security advisories for affected dependencies (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 7 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "CVE ID" · longest unbreakable word 46px · one-line width 125px
  col 2: header "Package" · longest unbreakable word 162px · one-line width 162px
  col 3: header "Affected versions" · longest unbreakable word 63px · one-line width 335px
  col 4: header "Severity" · longest unbreakable word 59px · one-line width 59px
  col 5: header "Summary" · longest unbreakable word 220px · one-line width 3094px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 360px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 359px.
This table cannot fit without splitting words at 360px. You MAY choose a total wider than 359px (the reader then scrolls horizontally), or squeeze and accept splits — a design decision.
Rendering convention: the screenshot always shows the WHOLE table. Anything beyond the dashed box is not clipped; it is the part a reader reaches by scrolling sideways, so judge both what fits in the box at first sight and the cost of scrolling to the rest.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 360px (different strategies, not small variations).
Reply ONLY JSON: {"understanding":{"purpose":"","reading":"","groups":["columns that belong together and why"],"keep_intact":[""],"may_wrap":[""]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[int px per column, column 1 first],"idea":"one sentence"}]}

log.raw: {"understanding":{"purpose":"Help readers identify security advisories affecting their dependencies and assess their severity and impact.","reading":"Readers scan package names and version ranges to find relevant dependencies, then compare severity and consult the CVE ID and summary for details. Summary wrapping can set the row height, leaving room for other cells to wrap without necessarily making the row taller.","groups":["CVE ID and severity identify and prioritize each advisory.","Package and affected versions work together to determine whether a dependency is affected.","Summary explains the impact of the advisory identified by the other columns."],"keep_intact":["CVE identifiers and package names, especially path-like names","Individual version numbers and comparison operators","Severity labels"],"may_wrap":["Affected-version expressions at spaces or between separate constraints","Summaries at natural word boundaries","Multiword headers"]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[146,183,180,80,260],"idea":"Preserve identifiers, package names and severity labels while giving version ranges and summaries room to wrap naturally, accepting substantial horizontal scrolling."},{"name":"B","widths":[146,125,120,80,160],"idea":"Keep CVE IDs and severity intact in a narrower scrolling table, while allowing long package names and version expressions to split and summaries to wrap."},{"name":"C","widths":[75,75,76,65,68],"idea":"Fit the entire table within the viewport so every column is visible at once, accepting frequent splits in identifiers, package names and summary text."}]}
